title: Berkshire 2000 letter: buying whole businesses, float economics, Aesop's value formula, and bubble-era speculation
summary: Buffett's 2000 letter explains why Berkshire prefers buying whole businesses to stocks, how to judge an insurer (float, its cost, and outlook), and the single value formula behind all investing. He also criticizes bubble speculation, earnings guidance, and corporate refusal to review failed decisions, while owning up to mistakes at GEICO and Dexter.

principles.text: Judge an insurer by float generated, its cost, and the long-term outlook for both; float is only valuable if it costs less than other money.
principles.quote: The key determinants are: (1) the amount of float that the business generates; (2) its cost; and (3) most critical of all, the long-term outlook for both of these factors.

principles.text: All assets bought for financial gain are valued by Aesop's formula: certainty, timing and amount of future cash, discounted at the risk-free rate.
principles.quote: How certain are you that there are indeed birds in the bush? When will they emerge and how many will there be? What is the risk-free interest rate

principles.text: Growth and value are not opposing styles; growth is just a component of value and can destroy it if it needs more cash than it returns.
principles.quote: Growth is simply a component  usually a plus, sometimes a minus  in the value equation.

principles.text: Speculation is most dangerous when it looks easiest; easy money sedates rationality and bubbles transfer wealth rather than create value.
principles.quote: Nothing sedates rationality like large doses of effortless money.

principles.text: Prefer sellers who love their business and care who buys it; that attachment signals honest accounting, pride of product and loyal people.
principles.quote: We like to do business with someone who loves his company, not just the money that a sale will bring him

principles.text: Acknowledge and analyze mistakes candidly; boardrooms rarely do post-mortems and instead bury blunders in 'nonrecurring' charges.
principles.quote: Agonizing over errors is a mistake. But acknowledging and analyzing them can be useful, though that practice is rare in corporate boardrooms.
